text:
ConocoPhillips fell 1.6% today to $127.30, extending a two-week decline as oil prices remain under pressure from easing geopolitical tension. Earlier in the week, U.S. crude dropped nearly 8% after Iran and the U.S. held talks at the U.N., with Iran proposing a conditional ceasefire—a development that typically weighs on energy stocks because it reduces the risk premium in oil prices. Though Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal on September 26th suggests renewed tension ahead, the market appears to be pricing in the possibility of diplomatic resolution rather than escalation.

The weakness is also framed by a broader shift in how investors are treating oil as an asset. Rather than a pure play on geopolitical risk, oil is increasingly seen as a hedge against supply shocks and inflation in a resource-constrained world—a more fundamental, less volatile thesis that can coexist with periods of diplomatic calm. With Saudi crude exports hitting their highest level since the Iran conflict began despite pipeline attacks, global supply concerns are easing, which removes some of the upside pressure on prices that would benefit an integrated oil producer like ConocoPhillips.
